top_comments.text: REA uses actual decompilers to read code instructions, that's why it takes longer but also produces better results, if you vibe it the model is just guessing, using REA it reads actual instructions, passes it to a tester and compares, if the results are not the same it decompiles again until it gets it exact, so you can recreate features faithfully with enough time. it's most impactful in things like device emulation, where exactness is a must, if you're just copying a feature then yeah, it doesn't have to be exact byte for byte like you would get from REA

The flip side is what I keep thinking about. If agents can take apart almost any app, the boundary that matters in your own setup is what they can never change.

I run a one-person firm on Claude Code agents. They check live data, write the reports and prepare decisions, but trading code, its config and anything that moves money sit in a zone no agent can edit without my sign-off, however urgent. When a strategy hit its pre-set limit in September, the system halted on its own, and restarting it still needs me.

Agents get more capable every month. The list of what they can't touch is the part I actually control.

The useful question for teams is what happens when the inputs stop being clean. That is usually where an AI workflow proves itself.

Tip: make the agent write its full plan to a markdown file before it touches anything, then run a second pass whose whole job is to poke holes in the plan. First drafts are always wrong. That file also doubles as the agent's memory, so after its context compacts it can re-read the file and recover everything. A skill that reverse-engineers in one shot is a great ingredient, but the loop is what makes it a recipe.
